claim: ATXN1 oligomers are the primary drivers of toxicity in Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1).
source: Previously, we reported that ATXN1 oligomers are the primary drivers of toxicity in Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1; Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2015)

claim: PolyQ ATXN1 oligomers can propagate locally in vivo in mice predisposed to SCA1 following intracerebral oligomeric tissue inoculation.
source: Here we report that polyQ ATXN1 oligomers can propagate locally in vivo in mice predisposed to SCA1 following intracerebral oligomeric tissue inoculation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from intracerebral injection studies presented in the manuscript

claim: Targeting ATXN1 oligomers with passive immunotherapy leads to some improvement in motor coordination in SCA1 mice.
source: Our data also show that targeting these oligomers with passive immunotherapy leads to some improvement in motor coordination in SCA1 mice and to a modest increase in their life span.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from immunotherapy studies and rotarod assays presented in the manuscript

claim: Targeting ATXN1 oligomers with passive immunotherapy leads to a modest increase in life span of SCA1 mice.
source: Our data also show that targeting these oligomers with passive immunotherapy leads to some improvement in motor coordination in SCA1 mice and to a modest increase in their life span.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from survival studies presented in the manuscript

claim: Oligomer propagation is regionally limited in SCA1.
source: These findings provide evidence that oligomer propagation is regionally limited in SCA1 and that immunotherapy targeting extracellular oligomers can mildly modify disease phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing oligomers only in cerebellum and brain stem, not in distant regions

claim: Immunotherapy targeting extracellular oligomers can mildly modify disease phenotypes in SCA1.
source: These findings provide evidence that oligomer propagation is regionally limited in SCA1 and that immunotherapy targeting extracellular oligomers can mildly modify disease phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from immunotherapy studies showing modest improvements

claim: Soluble oligomers play an important role in Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1).
source: We recently demonstrated that soluble oligomers play an important role in Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1), a neurodegenerative disease caused by expansion of a CAG repeat that encodes for glutamine (Q) in ataxin-1 (ATXN1)(Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2015)

claim: SCA1 is a neurodegenerative disease caused by expansion of a CAG repeat that encodes for glutamine (Q) in ataxin-1 (ATXN1).
source: We recently demonstrated that soluble oligomers play an important role in Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1), a neurodegenerative disease caused by expansion of a CAG repeat that encodes for glutamine (Q) in ataxin-1 (ATXN1)(Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2015).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about SCA1 and supported by citation

claim: ATXN1 oligomers are internalized into the cell and seed the formation of new ATXN1 oligomers.
source: In the same study, we showed that ATXN1 oligomers are internalized into the cell and seed the formation of new ATXN1 oligomers (Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2015)

claim: The 'seeding' concept has been explored in several other proteinopathies and is believed to be one of the drivers of neurodegeneration.
source: This 'seeding' concept has been explored in several other proteinopathies and is believed to be one of the drivers of neurodegeneration (Frost et al., 2009; Munch et al., 2011; Holmes and Diamond, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies (Frost et al., 2009; Munch et al., 2011; Holmes and Diamond, 2012)

claim: Soluble aggregates of amyloidogenic proteins including Tau, Aβ and α–synuclein can propagate pathology from cell-to-cell in a prion-like fashion.
source: What's more, evidence has mounted that soluble aggregates of amyloidogenic proteins including Tau, Aβ and α–synuclein, can propagate pathology from cell-to-cell in a prion-like fashion, thereby causing pathology progression from one brain region to the another in a disease-specific pattern (Hardy and Revesz, 2012; Holmes and Diamond, 2012; Guo and Lee, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies (Hardy and Revesz, 2012; Holmes and Diamond, 2012; Guo and Lee, 2014)

claim: Passive immunotherapy has been recently proposed as a feasible strategy to inhibit pathology propagation in mouse models for proteinopathy.
source: Passive immunotherapy has been recently proposed as a feasible strategy to inhibit pathology propagation in mouse models for proteinopathy (Banks et al., 2007; Chai et al., 2011; Masliah et al., 2011; Yanamandra et al., 2013; Castillo-Carranza et al., 2014; Games et al., 2014; Tran et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies (Banks et al., 2007; Chai et al., 2011; Masliah et al., 2011; Yanamandra et al., 2013; Castillo-Carranza et al., 2014; Games et al., 2014; Tran et al., 2014)

claim: It is not clear whether a mostly nuclear protein like ATXN1 will propagate from cell-to-cell in vivo.
source: Despite these advances, it is not clear whether a mostly nuclear protein like ATXN1 will propagate from cell-to-cell in vivo and whether passive immunotherapy targeting oligomers will modify disease course.
evidence: Represents a knowledge gap that motivates the current study

claim: It is not clear whether passive immunotherapy targeting oligomers will modify disease course in SCA1.
source: Despite these advances, it is not clear whether a mostly nuclear protein like ATXN1 will propagate from cell-to-cell in vivo and whether passive immunotherapy targeting oligomers will modify disease course.
evidence: Represents a knowledge gap that motivates the current study

claim: In Atxn1154Q/+ mice, ATXN1 oligomers are restricted to focal sub-populations of Purkinje cells (PCs) and are not evenly present throughout the cerebellum.
source: We recently demonstrated that in Atxn1154Q/+mice ATXN1 oligomers are restricted to focal sub-populations of Purkinje cells (PCs) and are not evenly present throughout the cerebellum.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2015)

claim: The focal distribution of ATXN1 oligomers in Atxn1154Q/+ mice coincided with cellular toxicity.
source: Notably, this focal distribution coincided with cellular toxicity (Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2015)

claim: Cerebellar extract from Atxn1154Q/+ mice is enriched in oligomers.
source: Before performing injections, we confirmed by western blot analysis that the injected material from Atxn1154Q/+mouse cerebella was indeed enriched in oligomers (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Cerebellar extracts from SCA1 Atxn1154Q/+ mice caused a two-to-three fold increase in oligomer formation in the cerebellum and brain stem of Atxn178Q/+ mice compared to other groups.
source: Three months after injection, ELISA revealed that cerebellar extracts from the SCA1 Atxn1154Q/+ mice caused a two-to-three fold increase in oligomer formation in the cerebellum and brain stem of Atxn178Q/+mice compared to other groups (Figure 1C, left panels).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Oligomer levels in the cortex did not significantly change in any of the groups following injection of cerebellar lysate.
source: Oligomer levels in the cortex, which were lower to begin with than in the cerebellum and brainstem, did not significantly change in any of the groups following injection of cerebellar lysate.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data presented in the manuscript

claim: Neuropathology confirmed that oligomers were located in cerebellum and brain stem, but not in cortex, hippocampus, striatum or olfactory bulb.
source: Neuropathology confirmed that oligomers were located in cerebellum and brain stem, but not in cortex, hippocampus, striatum or olfactory bulb (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by neuropathological examination data

claim: ATXN1 oligomers appear to propagate only to neighboring areas under the experimental conditions used.
source: ATXN1 oligomers thus appear to propagate only to neighboring areas, and, at least under these conditions, trans-synaptic propagation was not detected.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that oligomers were only found in cerebellum and brain stem, not distant regions

claim: Trans-synaptic propagation of ATXN1 oligomers was not detected under the experimental conditions used.
source: ATXN1 oligomers thus appear to propagate only to neighboring areas, and, at least under these conditions, trans-synaptic propagation was not detected.
evidence: Supported by the absence of oligomers in distant brain regions that would indicate trans-synaptic spread

claim: A higher concentration of inoculum and/or a longer incubation time might lead to oligomer propagation to farther areas.
source: Nevertheless, we can't exclude the possibility that a higher concentration of inoculum and/or a longer incubation time might lead to oligomer propagation to farther areas.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential alternative experimental conditions

claim: Similar amounts of total ATXN1 were observed in all groups of mice tested.
source: In all of the groups of mice tested, we observed similar amounts of total ATXN1 (Figure 1C, right panels), which indicates that the increase of oligomers in the cerebellum and brain stem of Atxn178Q/+mice was produced by a seeding effect of ATXN1-154Q soluble oligomers rather than by inducing more expression of ATXN1-78Q.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The increase of oligomers in the cerebellum and brain stem of Atxn178Q/+ mice was produced by a seeding effect of ATXN1-154Q soluble oligomers rather than by inducing more expression of ATXN1-78Q.
source: In all of the groups of mice tested, we observed similar amounts of total ATXN1 (Figure 1C, right panels), which indicates that the increase of oligomers in the cerebellum and brain stem of Atxn178Q/+mice was produced by a seeding effect of ATXN1-154Q soluble oligomers rather than by inducing more expression of ATXN1-78Q.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that total ATXN1 levels remained constant while oligomer levels increased

claim: Cells exposed to injected material from Atxn1154Q/+ developed the largest proportion of oligomeric inclusions (37.25%) compared to cells incubated with material from wild type or non-treated groups.
source: In comparison with cells incubated with the injected material from wild type or non-treated group, the cells exposed only to the injected material from Atxn1154Q/+ developed the largest proportion of oligomeric inclusions (37.25%).
evidence: Supported by cell-based seeding assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: When cells were exposed to injected material from Atxn1154Q/+ pre-incubated with F11G3, the proportion of oligomeric inclusions (15.25%) did not increase in comparison with control groups.
source: Moreover, when cells were exposed to the injected material from Atxn1154Q/+ pre-incubated with F11G3, the proportion of oligomeric inclusions (15.25%) did not increase in comparison with the control groups thus suggesting that the active material in the injected lysate are the oligomers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by cell-based seeding assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The active material in the injected lysate from Atxn1154Q/+ mice are the oligomers.
source: Moreover, when cells were exposed to the injected material from Atxn1154Q/+ pre-incubated with F11G3, the proportion of oligomeric inclusions (15.25%) did not increase in comparison with the control groups thus suggesting that the active material in the injected lysate are the oligomers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that F11G3 antibody blocked the seeding effect

claim: Only PCs of Atxn178Q/+ knockin mice injected with cerebellar extract from Atxn1154Q/+ mice, not those injected with WT cerebellar extract, showed an increase in oligomers.
source: In addition, this oligomeric pathology did not result from the surgical procedure itself: only PCs of Atxn178Q/+knockin mice injected with cerebellar extract from Atxn1154Q/+ mice, not those injected with WT cerebellar extract, showed an increase in oligomers (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 1D

claim: No oligomers were detected in PCs from either wild-type or Atxn1 null mice injected with Atxn1154Q/+ lysates.
source: The observation that no oligomers were detected in PCs from either wild-type or Atxn1 null mice injected with Atxn1154Q/+ lysates suggests that host expression of polyQ-expanded ATXN1 is necessary for the de novo formation of ATXN1 oligomers in PCs.
evidence: Supported by histological data from the injection experiments

claim: Host expression of polyQ-expanded ATXN1 is necessary for the de novo formation of ATXN1 oligomers in PCs.
source: The observation that no oligomers were detected in PCs from either wild-type or Atxn1 null mice injected with Atxn1154Q/+ lysates suggests that host expression of polyQ-expanded ATXN1 is necessary for the de novo formation of ATXN1 oligomers in PCs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that oligomers only formed in mice expressing polyQ-expanded ATXN1

claim: The oligomers detected in Atxn178Q/+ PCs were ATXN1 oligomers.
source: Immunofluorescence confirmed that the oligomers detected in Atxn178Q/+PCs were indeed ATXN1 oligomers (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E

claim: The ATXN1 oligomers present in the injected material from Atxn1154Q/+ are responsible for inducing propagation of ATXN1 oligomers in Atxn178Q/+ mice.
source: Overall, these data suggest that the ATXN1 oligomers present in the injected material from Atxn1154Q/+ are responsible for inducing propagation of ATXN1 oligomers in Atxn178Q/+mice.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations including seeding assays and injection studies

claim: Other factors present in the inoculum may play an important role in promoting propagation.
source: Nevertheless, it is possible that other factors present in the inoculum play an important role in promoting propagation.
evidence: Speculative statement acknowledging alternative explanations

claim: There was no evidence of sustained motor deficit in the Atxn178Q/+ knockin mice injected with cerebellar extract from Atxn1154Q/+ mice.
source: To determine if oligomer propagation was accompanied by motor deficit, we performed the rotarod assay in mice harboring brain lysate for 3 months. Even though the performance varied during training, there was no evidence of sustained deficit in the Atxn178Q/+knockin mice injected with cerebellar extract from Atxn1154Q/+ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by rotarod assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The newly formed 78Q ATXN1 oligomers appear insufficient to induce motor deficit or degeneration.
source: Despite the fact that oligomers propagate through the cerebellum in Atxn178Q/+knockin mice, the newly formed 78Q ATXN1 oligomers appear insufficient to induce motor deficit or degeneration (data not shown).
evidence: Inferred from the absence of motor deficits and degeneration despite oligomer propagation

claim: In Atxn178Q/+ knockin adult mice, the neurons are relatively healthy and thus can counteract the toxic effect of newly formed oligomers.
source: This lack of toxicity could be because in Atxn178Q/+knockin adult mice, the neurons are relatively healthy and thus can counteract the toxic effect of newly formed oligomers.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the lack of toxicity observed

claim: In Atxn1154Q/+ mice, the neurons become dysfunctional by four weeks.
source: In contrast, in Atxn1154Q/+mice, the neurons become dysfunctional by four weeks (Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2015) rendering them more susceptible to the toxicity of oligomers.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2015)

claim: Neurons in Atxn1154Q/+ mice are more susceptible to the toxicity of oligomers due to early dysfunction.
source: In contrast, in Atxn1154Q/+mice, the neurons become dysfunctional by four weeks (Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2015) rendering them more susceptible to the toxicity of oligomers.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that dysfunctional neurons are more vulnerable

claim: The newly formed 78Q ATXN1 oligomers may adopt a different structure or conformation that is less toxic than the 154Q ATXN1 oligomers.
source: Another possibility is that the newly formed 78Q ATXN1 oligomers adopt a different structure or conformation that is less toxic than the 154Q ATXN1 oligomers.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the lack of toxicity observed

claim: The anti-oligomer antibody F11G3 can inhibit the internalization of ATXN1 oligomer complexes from Atxn1154Q/+ cerebellum in vitro.
source: Given the ability of the anti-oligomer antibody F11G3 to inhibit the internalization of ATXN1 oligomer complexes from Atxn1154Q/+ cerebellum in vitro (Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2015), we postulated that anti-oligomer (F11G3) immunotherapy could reduce the load of ATXN1 oligomers and mitigate the motor impairment observed in the Atxn1154Q/+ model.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2015)

claim: Atxn1154Q/+ mice develop motor incoordination as early as 5 weeks of age.
source: Because Atxn1154Q/+ mice develop motor incoordination as early as 5 weeks of age (Watase et al., 2002), we began treatment at 4 weeks of age, where Atxn1154Q/+ mice already have a modest accumulation of oligomers in the cerebellum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Watase et al., 2002)

claim: At 4 weeks of age, Atxn1154Q/+ mice already have a modest accumulation of oligomers in the cerebellum.
source: Because Atxn1154Q/+ mice develop motor incoordination as early as 5 weeks of age (Watase et al., 2002), we began treatment at 4 weeks of age, where Atxn1154Q/+ mice already have a modest accumulation of oligomers in the cerebellum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Atxn1154Q/+ mice treated with the anti-oligomer antibody showed fewer PCs with oligomers than the control group.
source: Atxn1154Q/+ mice treated with the anti-oligomer antibody showed fewer PCs with oligomers than the control group (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: ELISA analysis showed a decrease in the amount of oligomers in cerebella of Atxn1154Q/+ mice following anti-oligomer immunotherapy.
source: We further analyzed the cerebella by ELISA and noted a decrease in the amount of oligomers and ATXN1 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2C

claim: ELISA analysis showed a decrease in the amount of ATXN1 in cerebella of Atxn1154Q/+ mice following anti-oligomer immunotherapy.
source: We further analyzed the cerebella by ELISA and noted a decrease in the amount of oligomers and ATXN1 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The immunotherapy did not affect the formation and total number of nuclear inclusions in the cortex.
source: Notably, the immunotherapy did not affect the formation and total number of nuclear inclusions in the cortex (Figure 2E): either these cortical inclusions are not preceded by oligomers or the antibody did not get internalized into these cells in vivo.
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Either cortical inclusions are not preceded by oligomers or the antibody did not get internalized into cortical cells in vivo.
source: Notably, the immunotherapy did not affect the formation and total number of nuclear inclusions in the cortex (Figure 2E): either these cortical inclusions are not preceded by oligomers or the antibody did not get internalized into these cells in vivo.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the lack of effect on cortical inclusions

claim: The anti-oligomer antibody arrests the propagation of ATXN1 oligomer complexes to neighboring areas by targeting extracellular oligomeric entities rather than directly targeting intracellular oligomers.
source: Considering our previous study where we demonstrated that the anti-oligomer antibody blocks the seeding effect of ATXN1 oligomers in cell culture without getting internalized into the cell (Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2015), we suggest that the anti-oligomer antibody arrests the propagation of ATXN1 oligomer complexes to neighboring areas by targeting extracellular oligomeric entities rather than directly targeting intracellular oligomers.
evidence: Inferred from prior work showing antibody blocks seeding without internalization and current immunotherapy results

claim: Western blot analysis revealed a decrease in ATXN1 oligomers in the treated group.
source: The western blot analysis revealed a decrease in ATXN1 oligomers in the treated group, but no observable change at the level of monomeric ATXN1 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: Western blot analysis showed no observable change at the level of monomeric ATXN1 following immunotherapy.
source: The western blot analysis revealed a decrease in ATXN1 oligomers in the treated group, but no observable change at the level of monomeric ATXN1 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: Rotarod analysis revealed a mildly significant improvement in coordination following six weeks of anti-oligomer immunotherapy.
source: To determine the functional consequences of this immunotherapy, we tested motor performance in treated and control Atxn1154Q/+ mice. Rotarod analysis revealed a mildly significant improvement in coordination following six weeks of anti-oligomer immunotherapy (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by rotarod assay data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Treated Atxn1154Q/+ mice still possessed a motor deficit in comparison with wild type mice.
source: Although treated mice still possessed a motor deficit in comparison with wild type mice, continued weekly immunotherapy treatments in Atxn1154Q/+ mice throughout their lifespan extended survival by approximately 3.5 weeks in comparison with the control-treated Atxn1154Q/+ mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by rotarod assay data

claim: Continued weekly immunotherapy treatments in Atxn1154Q/+ mice throughout their lifespan extended survival by approximately 3.5 weeks in comparison with control-treated Atxn1154Q/+ mice.
source: Although treated mice still possessed a motor deficit in comparison with wild type mice, continued weekly immunotherapy treatments in Atxn1154Q/+ mice throughout their lifespan extended survival by approximately 3.5 weeks in comparison with the control-treated Atxn1154Q/+ mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Amyloid formation is characterized by seeding.
source: It is widely accepted that amyloid formation is characterized by such seeding (Serio et al., 2000; Pedersen et al., 2004).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge and supported by citations (Serio et al., 2000; Pedersen et al., 2004)

claim: Extracellular aggregates that are internalized into the cell induce aggregation of intracellular proteins.
source: This phenomenon has been explored in cell culture assays, several of which have demonstrated that extracellular aggregates that are internalized into the cell induce aggregation of intracellular proteins (Frost et al., 2009; Munch et al., 2011; Holmes and Diamond, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies (Frost et al., 2009; Munch et al., 2011; Holmes and Diamond, 2012)

claim: The concept of cell-to-cell spread of many amyloidogenic proteins in vivo has been demonstrated by the progression of protein aggregate pathology from one brain region to another in a disease-specific pattern.
source: Moreover, the concept of cell-to-cell spread of many amyloidogenic proteins in vivo has been demonstrated by the progression of protein aggregate pathology from one brain region to another in a disease-specific pattern (Hardy and Revesz, 2012; Holmes and Diamond, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies (Hardy and Revesz, 2012; Holmes and Diamond, 2012)

claim: Injected oligomers induced formation of new ATXN1 oligomers only in areas proximal to the injection site.
source: In our study, however, we found that injected oligomers induced formation of new ATXN1 oligomers only in areas proximal to the injection site.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from injection studies

claim: It seems unlikely that ATXN1 oligomers propagate transsynaptically in SCA1.
source: It thus seems unlikely that ATXN1 oligomers propagate transsynaptically in SCA1, as has been suggested with other neurodegenerative diseases (Harris et al., 2010; de Calignon et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012; Pecho-Vrieseling et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that oligomers only spread locally, not to distant connected regions

claim: ATXN1 propagates through a secretion and reuptake mechanism between neighboring cells.
source: Rather, we suggest ATXN1 propagates through a secretion and reuptake mechanism between neighboring cells as has been proposed for other proteinopathies (Guo and Lee, 2014).
evidence: Inferred from the local spread pattern and supported by analogy to other proteinopathies

claim: No obvious signs of degeneration or motor incoordination were observed in the injected mice.
source: Furthermore, no obvious signs of degeneration or motor incoordination were observed in the injected mice.
evidence: Supported by behavioral and pathological data from injection experiments

claim: The cell must continuously express the toxic entity to trigger degeneration and behavioral deficits in mice.
source: This suggests that the cell must continuously express the toxic entity to trigger degeneration and behavioral deficits in mice.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that injected oligomers alone did not cause degeneration or motor deficits

claim: The antibody hindered the local propagation of ATXN1 oligomers.
source: This notion is supported by the observation that immunotherapy targeting the ATXN1 oligomers slightly modified the phenotype in the Atxn1154Q/+ mice: the antibody hindered the local propagation of ATXN1 oligomers.
evidence: Supported by immunotherapy experimental data

claim: The immunotherapy treatment is not curative because neurons expressing polyQ ATXN1 will still form their own toxic oligomeric entities.
source: This treatment is not curative, however, because neurons expressing polyQ ATXN1 will still form their own toxic oligomeric entities, and some non-oligomeric forms of PolyQ ATXN1 might contribute to toxicity.
evidence: Inferred from the modest effects of immunotherapy and understanding of disease mechanism

claim: Some non-oligomeric forms of PolyQ ATXN1 might contribute to toxicity.
source: This treatment is not curative, however, because neurons expressing polyQ ATXN1 will still form their own toxic oligomeric entities, and some non-oligomeric forms of PolyQ ATXN1 might contribute to toxicity.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential alternative toxic species

claim: Passive immunotherapy might slightly impact disease progression by blocking the propagation of oligomeric entities.
source: Our findings suggest that such therapy might slightly impact disease progression by blocking the propagation of these oligomeric entities, but to halt or reverse symptoms it would likely be necessary to incorporate a joint therapy that targets the root cause of disease, the abnormal accumulation of polyQ ATXN1 (Park et al., 2013).
evidence: Inferred from the modest therapeutic effects observed in the study

claim: To halt or reverse symptoms it would likely be necessary to incorporate a joint therapy that targets the root cause of disease, the abnormal accumulation of polyQ ATXN1.
source: Our findings suggest that such therapy might slightly impact disease progression by blocking the propagation of these oligomeric entities, but to halt or reverse symptoms it would likely be necessary to incorporate a joint therapy that targets the root cause of disease, the abnormal accumulation of polyQ ATXN1 (Park et al., 2013).
evidence: Inferred from the limited efficacy of immunotherapy alone and supported by citation

claim: ATXN1 oligomer propagation contributes to SCA1 pathogenesis.
source: Altogether, our findings revealed that ATXN1 oligomer propagation contributes to SCA1 pathogenesis, and that such propagation especially in the vicinity of affected cells, could be targeted through passive immunotherapy.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from injection and immunotherapy studies

claim: ATXN1 oligomer propagation, especially in the vicinity of affected cells, could be targeted through passive immunotherapy.
source: Altogether, our findings revealed that ATXN1 oligomer propagation contributes to SCA1 pathogenesis, and that such propagation especially in the vicinity of affected cells, could be targeted through passive immunotherapy.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from immunotherapy studies

claim: The benefit from passive immunotherapy was small.
source: That the benefit from such therapy was small highlights the need to develop therapies that target ATXN1, the protein driving the pathogenesis.
evidence: Supported by the modest improvements observed in motor coordination and survival

claim: There is a need to develop therapies that target ATXN1, the protein driving the pathogenesis.
source: That the benefit from such therapy was small highlights the need to develop therapies that target ATXN1, the protein driving the pathogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the limited efficacy of immunotherapy targeting oligomers

claim: The need for combination therapy is likely to extend to other disease-driving proteins.
source: The need for such combination therapy is likely to extend to other disease-driving proteins.
evidence: Speculative generalization based on findings in SCA1

claim: Atxn178Q/+ mice express one allele of murine Atxn1 with a 78Q expansion.
source: Atxn178Q/+mice express one allele of murine Atxn1 with a 78Q expansion.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about this mouse model

claim: Atxn178Q/+ mice do not display behavioral abnormalities nor any neuropathology, including ATXN1 inclusions.
source: These mice do not display behavioral abnormalities nor any neuropathology, including ATXN1 inclusions, indicating that a single copy of 78Q-Atxn1 is insufficient to generate disease within the short lifespan of a mouse (Lorenzetti et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Lorenzetti et al., 2000)

claim: A single copy of 78Q-Atxn1 is insufficient to generate disease within the short lifespan of a mouse.
source: These mice do not display behavioral abnormalities nor any neuropathology, including ATXN1 inclusions, indicating that a single copy of 78Q-Atxn1 is insufficient to generate disease within the short lifespan of a mouse (Lorenzetti et al., 2000).
evidence: Inferred from the absence of pathology in Atxn178Q/+ mice and supported by citation

claim: Atxn178Q/+ mice are an ideal model to determine the seeding abilities of ATXN1 soluble oligomers from Atxn1154Q/+ mice lysates.
source: These characteristics make this mouse an ideal model to determine the seeding abilities of ATXN1 soluble oligomers from Atxn1154Q/+mice lysates.
evidence: Inferred from the characteristics of Atxn178Q/+ mice that make them suitable for seeding experiments

claim: Atxn1154Q/+, Atxn178Q/+ and Atxn1-/- mice have been previously described and were backcrossed to C57BL/6 for more than ten generations.
source: Atxn1154Q/+,Atxn178Q/+ and Atxn1-/- mice have been previously described (Lorenzetti et al., 2000; Watase et al., 2002) and were backcrossed to C57BL/6 for more than ten generations.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Lorenzetti et al., 2000; Watase et al., 2002)
